title: What is Zen, Part 4
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna and Reizan Bob Penny
summary: The speaker emphasizes the importance of approaching conflicts and imperfections with sincerity and openness, rather than seeking a state of constant peace and happiness. They share their personal experience of finding a more honest community in Zen Buddhism, where mistakes are acknowledged and grown from, and encourage the audience to use available resources to work through their own differences and make good use of their "messy stories" in history. By practicing conflict resolution tools like nonviolent communication and anchoring, individuals can cultivate cooperative energy and soften their approach to resolve conflicts in a way that is honest and non-blaming.

**Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna:** I'm hoping it doesn't work.
Ken said there might be a problem with it.
Anyway, thanks for being here.
This is our last class in this Dharma Seminar Series, so next week we'll return to a normal schedule.
Some of you don't know what a normal schedule is.
Sometimes we don't either, but we expect it to be done with us tonight.
Bob and I are still working on Norman's book, *What Is Zen?*, and we're taking the chapter on everyday life and relationships.
We'll be focusing more specifically on conflict, institutional conflict as well as personal conflict.
And also we'll engage a little bit in sangha conflict.
So it should be spicy.
It is really easy these days to feel like we are surrounded by conflict.
Even if we aren't, if we're trying to ignore the news, it exists on the subliminal level for, I think, all of us.
Plus, no matter what is happening, history proves that human needs will always be in conflict.
Yet for some reason in the human psyche we keep looking for, and we keep expecting, some state where all our needs will constantly be filled.
Otherwise why would we get irritated or frustrated?
We think maybe some white knight will appear and clean up all our messes.
Many people come to relationships, and especially to spiritual communities, looking for and expecting just this: that everything will be okay.
But religion, and that includes Buddhism, seems to promise so much, so it's reasonable, I guess, to have that expectation when we talk about things like enlightenment.
We talk about the second noble truth, which is the cessation of suffering.
And we talk about states of joy and bliss, and if not here then maybe in another life.
But there's always the other side.
We will have bad days.
We will have aches and pains, irritations.
Maybe we'll get depressed or lonely.
And all our neuroses do not drop away when we walk into the Zendo.
Sorry.
So the dark spots taint every institution, every major religion, and every individual soul.
I grew up in the Catholic Church, and so of course I've seen a lot of denial of this.
I was thinking about the textbooks that we used to use.
I went to Catholic school, and on the front cover of every textbook there was this, and those of you who went to Catholic school are familiar with it: an [unclear: "impromata"], imprimatur.
The imprimatur, it's hard for me to...
I forgot my Latin, this is the problem.
It's the official sanction from the Catholic Church that what you're reading is according to doctrine.
And we're not going to deviate from any of the doctrine here.
I remember specifically reading about the Crusades, and how the Crusades, of course, were called a holy war.
At that time I was a kid and I believed all this.
I believed that there would be salvation if you went to war and you killed thousands of people.
What we didn't talk about were a number of things.
The Inquisition, we didn't talk about.
If you're familiar with church history, there's this whole string of corrupt popes.
Of course, we didn't talk about them.
And now there's this sex abuse scandal making the news.
All that was buried.

I was led to believe also, and it wasn't an overt kind of teaching, but it rose up subtly through childhood, that I and my Catholic schoolmates were somehow better, maybe more pure than our public school neighbors.
We would never wear makeup or tease our hair or French kiss in the back of some dude's Chevy.
We just wouldn't do that stuff like those hussies and hoodlums were doing.
I held on to this kind of thinking until about my mid-teens and then turned around by about 180 degrees.
By the time I came to Buddhism, I had really been around the block with a number of different spiritual communities.
I'd seen some inspiring, but also demoralizing, behaviors in those communities.
At that time, maybe more so than now, although this still happens, traditions from other cultures were really so romanticized.
We felt like they were very exotic and very alluring.
And the spiritual teachers and leaders were placed up very high on a pedestal, not human anymore.
What this leads to is blinding people to any inappropriate behaviors.
They can be harmful behaviors, and that tendency makes people not see what's going on.
So when I finally came to Zen, I did approach the practice with some skepticism and some reserve, with this history in my background.
But then early on in my Zen practice, I listened to a Dharma talk by Norman Fischer, where he brought up some serious contemporary breaches of ethics within the Zen community.
This is the broader community, not our smaller sanghas, not here, not like Mountain Rain, but bigger teachers and bigger names.
I thought, oh, sure, here we go again, but it was different this time.
Instead of whitewashing, Norman was brokenhearted.
He was quite upset and he made no excuses.
He made no justifications for any of these people or for any of their actions.
So, of course, after that I had to go home and get on my computer and look up other stuff, and I did, and I researched it.
I saw, for example, that in early Buddhism there's a lot of conflict and fighting between different schools of Buddhism.
This was even prior to Zen.
And then, for those of you who are aware of this, there was the militarism of the Zen Buddhist establishment during World War Two.
That's a really tragic and sorry history.
What I do understand now about that was that in about 2000, 2001, 2002, these communities made public apologies.
They put out letters and put out apologies.
They came to some acknowledgement and recognition of what they had been involved in.
And then, of course, let's see.
Oh, I also researched the sexual exploits of some of our contemporary Buddhist teachers, and they're out there.
But I wasn't shocked and I wasn't even dismayed.

What gave me hope and confidence was the honesty and the humility and the courage of a leader in a community that could look at its own mistakes without rationalizing or making excuses this time, and then even going farther and acknowledging the harm and using that for healing and for growth in the community.
For me, this was like a huge relief.
It was such a contrast to my past.
And I thought, okay, I can be with this community.
I can be with that level of honesty and openness.
So what I'm saying today is not to get you interested in all these salacious stories, and they're out there, or into gossip about misguided Zen teachers.
Certainly, I am not intending to disparage our tradition.
I believe, and I have seen, that these tragic episodes are really outweighed by so much good in our practice.
But what I really hope to do is to inspire you by the sincerity and the openness that is modeled in our sanghas.

My practice and my resolve, my intention to actually live deeper into the precepts and to make right the wrong of our history, was really strengthened by learning about the confused and conflicted behaviors of the past, and then the communities' response to them.
So I want to add here that our little Red Cedar Zen community, once called Bellingham Zen, has survived since 1991 without any major ethical breaches.
So we can give ourselves a hand here.
That's not to deny that there have been some disagreements and some misunderstandings between individuals.

It's true.

They've encouraged our communities to put tools in place that help us confront misunderstandings before they get out of hand: the preventive procedures.

We've always had the silence of sitting to look deeply and honestly into ourselves.
So I'm urging all of you to take advantage of these resources.
I'm also encouraging us to make good use of these messy stories in our history, just as we would face with courage those hidden and unpleasant demons in our own hearts and minds.

So in this book that we've been doing our trainings on this month, Norman talks about many questions that just come up for people who are new to Zen practice, or maybe who have been doing it a long time.
In this chapter that we're looking at, he has a quote.
And he says:
*The foundational idea we work with at Everyday Zen is that Zen practice isn't what happens in the zendo, the monastery or when you come to hear teachings or participate in ceremonies.
All those activities support and encourage the actual practice, which happens all the time in your own life, in your every encounter with others, in your heart and mind.
Everyday Zen means that everyday life really is your practice.
And naturally, this includes your work and your family life.*
The chapter continues, and there are a couple of good extended questions in there about how you bring up your complaints, especially in light of some of our precepts about speech.
Norman gives answers that weigh heavily towards upholding the precept we have of not speaking ill of others.

I find that precept pretty powerful for myself, because through practicing it I often find that the complaint I have in my head is really my problem and not the problem of the person I'm thinking I have the complaint about.
That insight comes to me through the process of not acting on the impulse to complain.
Norman says about this:
*People hurt each other all the time with their sloppy and unkind speech.
As much as we are inured to it, we are also deep inside hurt by it and become wary and mistrustful of each other.
If I make belittling remarks about you to others when you are not around, why would I think you'll do any different with me?
Maybe I can only trust my very best friends, and even sometimes not them.*
So I think we see this precept as an ideal which can guide our approach to dealing with conflict.
With that perspective in mind, we can actually work in everyday life to address complaints and problems we have with others which seem to be perennial and not passing impressions.
We have to get along with each other, and sometimes maybe our complaining mind could simply be seen as an indicator that a situation needs to be attended to on some level.
So a corollary to the absolute expression of that precept of not discussing the faults of others could perhaps be a relative expression:
*Admit our complaints and work to resolve them with no blame to ourselves or others.
Certainly complaining to third parties is generally unproductive.
But there are times when it would be best to present complaints to those involved.

In those cases we have the option to choose to enter into a process to resolve conflict with another, not with blame but with an awareness of the two-way street involved in relationships, that we are every bit as much a part of whatever that conflictual situation is as the other person.*
